newsitem.title: yugoslavia: Serbian protests resume, students chase minister.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protests resume, students chase minister.

text.p: The Serbian opposition resumed daily demonstrations on Wednesday, getting support from two U.S. senators at one rally while students chased the Serbian education minister down the street at another.

Some 20,000 to 30,000 supporters of the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) gathered at a square in the capital Belgrade to hear fiery speeches denouncing President Slobodan Milosevic and expressions of support from the U.S. Senators on the 59th day of protests across Serbia.
The main demand is the restoration of annulled November 17 municipal elections in which opposition candidates won 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities.

A block away, several thousand students waiting outside the university rectorate were shocked when they learned that one of their principal demands, the sacking of rector Dragutin Velickovic, had been rejected by the university council.
The noisy crowd of students had waited all day for Velickovic to emerge but when Education Minister Dragoslav Mladenovic came out instead they chased him.
With the aid of security guards, Mladenovic took refuge in a nearby headquarters building of the Socialist Party.

"Students are disappointed both by the duplicity of the university council and that of the Serbian deputy prime ministers," student spokesman Cedmoir Jovanovic said, referring to a weekend statement in which the deputy prime ministers said student demands would be fulfilled.
"All members of the university council must realise that we are made of material that is a little tougher than velvet and that we shall continue to protest," Jovanovic said at a news conference.

At the Zajedno rally, the first since a half million people turned out for Orthodox New Year's Eve, U.S. Democratic Senators Carl Levin of Michigan and Jack Reed of Rhode Island expressed strong support for the pro-democracy demonstrators.

"We salute those people who peacefully seek democracy and work for a democratic Serbia that is ruled by law and which is at peace with its neighbours and itself," said Levin who is the senior Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
Reed told the crowd: "We salute you for your brave struggle for democracy.
"You have chosen a difficult path but there is no turning back," Reed said. "Americans stand with you because you stand for democracy."
The two senators spoke after holding talks with Milan Milutinovic, foreign minister of federal Yugoslavia which groups Serbia and tiny Montenegro, and with Army Chief of Staff Momcilo Perisic.
Reed said they had discussed the Dayton peace accords and the resettlement of refugees and had commended the military "on staying out of this political trouble".

The demonstrators, who took Tuesday afternoon off after the Orthodox New Year, remained extremely sceptical about announcements that electoral commissions had restored their victories in Belgrade and Nis.

"We want our victory in its entirety," Zoran Djindjic, the Democratic Party head and a Zajedno leader, told the crowd. "No horsetrading, Mr President. The November 17 results are sacred to the democratic opposition...
"Things are beginning to crash down about his head," Djindjic added. "We don't believe that it is a matter of any sensible politics on their part, they're panicking...
As he spoke scores of buses full of riot police were heading towards Belgrade from the countryside, witnesses said.
